header: Deterministic term/date parsing for holiday queries. No AI. I mirror the employees parser's style: plain regex plus a small curated map, grounded in the live corpus (scripts/probe-holidays.mjs, scripts/probe-holidays-battery.mjs). Enum ground truth (confirmed against the live DB, 2026-09-21 probe): CH = Closed Holiday (mandatory, non-optional -- Independence Day, Republic Day, Gandhi Jayanti, May Day, SAIL Foundation Day). NOT "Compensated" -- the model file's inline comment is wrong. I fixed it here (the term mapping) and left it alone there: renaming that comment is cosmetic and out of scope for Stage 2. FH = Festival Holiday (fixed religious/festival calendar -- Diwali, Durga Puja tithis, Eid, Christmas, Good Friday, Janmashtami, etc.) RH = Restricted Holiday (the large optional pick-list -- Holi, Bengali New Year, various pujas, etc.)

symbols.name: TYPE_LABEL
symbols.sig: const TYPE_LABEL: Record<HolidayType, string> = { [HolidayType.CH]: "Closed", [HolidayType.FH]: "Festival", [HolidayType.RH]: "Restricted", }

symbols.name: CATEGORY_LABEL
symbols.sig: const CATEGORY_LABEL: Record<"A" | "B" | "C" | "D", string> = { A: "Executives (Works & Non-Works)", B: "Non-industrial non-executives (Offices, Education Deptt & Kolkata Branch) …
doc: I confirmed this from the actual holiday-list circulars for every seeded year (2020-2026): this exact category table (name + description) appears verbatim at the top of each one, unchanged year to year. It is not derived and not guessed, it is copied from source.

symbols.name: resolveHolidayType
symbols.sig: export function resolveHolidayType(normalizedText: string): HolidayType | null
doc: I resolve a free-text holiday-type mention to its enum, or return null if none is found.

symbols.name: CATEGORY_RE
symbols.sig: const CATEGORY_RE = /\bcat(?:egory)?\b[.\s-]*([a-z0-9]+)\b/gi
doc: Employee category (A/B/C/D) -- as distinct from HolidayType (CH/FH/RH). I need it for questions like "how many RH can Category B take" or "which FH does Category A get", which filter by WHO the entitlement applies to, not by which kind of holiday it is.

I require "cat" / "category" to be a WHOLE word, so "categories", "catering" or "catalogue" can never be read as "cat" + a token (that is how "which categories get it" used to become "Category EGORIES is not valid").

symbols.name: NOT_A_CATEGORY_TOKEN
symbols.sig: const NOT_A_CATEGORY_TOKEN = new Set([ "of", "is", "are", "was", "were", "wise", "gets", "get", "getting", "can", "could", "does", "do", "did", " …
doc: These are ordinary English words that naturally follow the word "category" ("which category gets Diwali", "category wise quota", "category of employees"). They are NOT an attempt to name a category. I still treat a token outside this list (z, 5, ab, abc ...) as an attempted category, and I reject it loudly.

symbols.name: VALID_CATEGORIES
symbols.sig: const VALID_CATEGORIES = new Set(["A", "B", "C", "D"])

symbols.name: CategoryResolution
symbols.sig: | { valid: true; category: string } | { valid: false; input: string }
doc: The result of trying to resolve a "Category X" mention: either a real, known category (A-D), or an explicit mention of something that ISN'T one (e.g. "category Z", "category 5", "category abc"). I never let these two cases be conflated. Conflating them (treating an unrecognized token the same as "no category was mentioned at all") would silently answer a nonsense category as if it were an unfiltered query -- see resolveCategory's docstring below.

symbols.name: resolveCategory
symbols.sig: export function resolveCategory(normalizedText: string): CategoryResolution | null
doc: I resolve a free-text "Category X" mention to its single-letter code, or flag it as invalid, or return null if no "cat"/"category" mention exists in the text at all. It accepts "category b", "cat b", "cat. b", "category-b", case-insensitively. A valid category is always returned as the uppercase letter, matching how categories are stored (holidayyear.categories, e.g. "A,B", and holiday_rh_quota.category).

The captured token is whatever whole word follows "cat"/"category" -- word-bounded on BOTH sides, not just a single character -- so "category b" (one letter) and "category abc" or "category 5" (not a single valid letter) are all recognized as an attempted category mention and can be told apart from each other. I do not let a multi-character token simply fail to match at all and silently fall back to null.

I keep "not mentioned" (null) apart from "mentioned but invalid" ({valid:false}) because it matters: a caller that only checked "is category truthy?" would treat "how many RH can category Z take" the same as a plain unfiltered "how many RH", silently answering a question that was never asked instead of saying Category Z doesn't exist.

symbols.name: parseMonthName
symbols.sig: export function parseMonthName(normalizedText: string): number | null

symbols.name: parseMonthNames
symbols.sig: export function parseMonthNames(normalizedText: string): number[]
doc: Returns all DISTINCT months named anywhere in the query, in the order first mentioned, for "holidays in March and April 2025" style queries. parseMonthName (singular) only ever looks at the first match; I use the same underlying regex here, just collecting every match instead of one.

symbols.name: tryParseOneDate
symbols.sig: function tryParseOneDate(fragment: string): SimpleDate | null
doc: I try to read ONE date out of a short fragment (already isolated by the caller -- see parseDateRange). Tries, in order: numeric "dd mm yyyy" (the shape normTerm produces from "10/03/2025" or "10-03-2025", since it turns "/" and "-" into spaces before this ever runs), "dd <month name> [yyyy]", and "<month name> dd [yyyy]". It returns null rather than guess if none of these three specific, well-defined shapes match: an unrecognized format should surface as "I couldn't read this date," never as a silently-wrong one.

symbols.name: DateRangeResult
symbols.sig: | { kind: "range"; from: SimpleDate; to: SimpleDate } | { kind: "ambiguous" } | { kind: "missing-year" } | null

symbols.name: RANGE_STRUCTURE_RE
symbols.sig: const RANGE_STRUCTURE_RE = /\b(from|between)\b.+\b(to|and|till|until)\b/

symbols.name: RANGE_LOOKS_DATE_SHAPED_RE
symbols.sig: const RANGE_LOOKS_DATE_SHAPED_RE = new RegExp( MONTH_WORD_RE.source + "|" + /\b\d{1,2}\s+\d{1,2}\s+\d{2,4}\b/.source,)
doc: I require something date-SHAPED to be present at all before treating a "from X to Y" query as a date-range attempt -- otherwise a perfectly ordinary "holidays from 2023 to 2025" (a bare year mention, not a date) would get intercepted here and reported as an unparseable range, when it was never meant to be one. This checks for a month name or a dd-mm-yy(yy)-shaped numeric triple; a bare 4-digit year alone doesn't count (it never has the internal spacing a 3-part triple needs). I deliberately widened it to 2-4 digit trailing numbers, not just 20xx: a genuine attempt at a date with a 2-digit year ("1/3/25 to 30/6/25") must still be recognized as a date-range ATTEMPT so it gets the explicit "couldn't read this, use dd/mm/yyyy" rejection. tryParseOneDate below still only accepts a full 4-digit year as valid, so this widening alone can't cause a 2-digit year to be silently accepted; it only prevents the query from being mistaken for "no range attempted at all" and silently falling through to a default full-year list instead of being rejected.

symbols.name: parseDateRange
symbols.sig: export function parseDateRange(normalizedText: string, now: DateTime): DateRangeResult
doc: I detect and parse an explicit custom date range ("from 10/03/2025 to 15/06/2025", "between 1st March and 30th June 2025"). It is deliberately narrow: only the three date shapes tryParseOneDate understands, and only within a single calendar year (see the caller in parser.ts for why a range spanning two years is reported as unsupported rather than silently mishandled). Both dates must state their own year explicitly; see "missing-year" above for why I never infer or default it.

symbols.name: RELATIVE_MONTHS_RE
symbols.sig: const RELATIVE_MONTHS_RE = /\b(next|previous)\s+(\d{1,2}|one|two|three|four|five|six|seven|eight|nine|ten|eleven|twelve)?\s*months?\b/

symbols.name: RelativeMonthsResult
symbols.sig: | { kind: "months"; year: number; months: number[] } | { kind: "cross-year"; wouldBeYear: number } | null

symbols.name: parseRelativeMonths
symbols.sig: export function parseRelativeMonths(normalizedText: string, now: DateTime): RelativeMonthsResult
doc: "next month" / "next 2 months" / "next three months" / "previous month" / "previous 4 months" are resolved relative to `now`'s month, always within `now`'s year. "Next month" means the single month right after the current one (not including the current month); "next 2 months" means the two months after that, and so on. The shape is the same for "previous."

symbols.name: parseExplicitDate
symbols.sig: export function parseExplicitDate( normalizedText: string,): { month: number; day: number; year: number | null } | null
symbols.returns: { month: number; day: number; year: number | null } | null
doc: Explicit day+month (+ optional year) extraction, e.g. "15 august", "august 15", "15th august 2026", "2026 08 15" (ISO -- normTerm turns "-"/"/" into spaces so "2026-08-15" arrives as "2026 08 15").

symbols.sig: const WEEKDAYS: Record<string, number> = { monday: 1, tuesday: 2, wednesday: 3, thursday: 4, friday: 5, saturday: 6, sunday: 7, }

symbols.name: parseRelativeDate
symbols.sig: export function parseRelativeDate(normalizedText: string, now: DateTime): DateTime | null

symbols.name: extractYears
symbols.sig: export function extractYears(normalizedText: string, now: DateTime): number[]
doc: Relative / explicit YEAR resolution ("this year", "last year", "2026", ...). Returns every year mentioned, in reading order, resolved to a concrete number via Luxon's current year. Callers still MUST check the year is actually loaded in holidayyear before answering from it: this function never invents data, it only resolves what the text says into a number.

symbols.name: HolidayNameRecord
doc: One holidaymaster row's canonical name plus any known alternate spellings (e.g. "Doljatra" carrying alias "Dol Yatra"). Aliases let a query using either spelling resolve to the same row -- see findHolidayNameInText.

symbols.name: nameCache
symbols.sig: const nameCache = new Map<number | "all", { records: HolidayNameRecord[]; at: number }>()

symbols.name: NAME_CACHE_TTL_MS
symbols.sig: const NAME_CACHE_TTL_MS = 5 * 60 * 1000

symbols.name: getHolidayNames
symbols.sig: export async function getHolidayNames(year?: number | null): Promise<HolidayNameRecord[]>
doc: I fetch known holiday names (+ aliases) for name matching. When `year` is given, results are scoped to holidaymaster rows that actually have a holidayyear instance that year. This is critical because this corpus's exact printed spelling for the same conceptual holiday genuinely drifts year to year (sometimes just whitespace, e.g. "Dashami / Dussehra" vs "Dashami/ Dussehra"; sometimes a real respelling, e.g. "Pongal" vs "Pongol"). An unscoped search across every year at once has no way to prefer the spelling that's actually correct for the year being asked about, and can resolve to a different year's variant entirely, which then fails to match anything when looked up against the year the person actually meant. When `year` is omitted (no year known yet, e.g. bare "when is Holi"), I fall back to the original unscoped, all-years search.

symbols.name: findHolidayNameInText
symbols.sig: export function findHolidayNameInText( normalizedQuery: string, names: HolidayNameRecord[],): string | null
doc: I find the longest name-or-alias that appears as a whole phrase in the query (case/punctuation-insensitive via normTerm on both sides). It mirrors findDepartmentInText's longest-match-wins approach. It requires >= 4 characters to avoid accidental short-token hits. It always returns the CANONICAL holidaymaster.name, even when what actually matched in the query text was one of that row's aliases, so every caller downstream (the hijack guard, and the name filter handed to queryHolidays' DB lookups, which match against the literal `name` column) keeps working against a real holidaymaster.name without needing to know aliases exist.

symbols.name: QUESTION_FRAME_WORDS
symbols.sig: const QUESTION_FRAME_WORDS = /\b(when|what|which|is|are|falls?|fall|falling|date|on|in|the|a|an|of)\b/g
doc: A small set of question-framing words that are never part of a holiday name. I strip them in addition to the domain scaffolding (type/year/month/day) so that what is left is name-shaped before it is handed to the phonetic function, which expects a name-like string, not a full sentence. I added "in" after a live bug: "when is shivaratri in 2024" strips the year via stripDomainScaffolding but left a dangling "in", producing the fragment "shivaratri in" instead of "shivaratri", which then fails to phonetically match "Maha Shivratri" (holiday_phonetic_match saw an extra stray word it was never meant to encode). Confirmed live in the app (Stage 4 Step 3 test): the query fell through to circular search instead of resolving via the phonetic layer. The root cause was this preposition never being in the strip list, not the phonetic function itself.

symbols.name: HOLIDAY_WORD_LOCAL
symbols.sig: const HOLIDAY_WORD_LOCAL = /\bholidays?\b/
doc: This is a local copy of parser.ts's HOLIDAY_WORD. terms.ts can't import it back from parser.ts (parser.ts already imports from terms.ts; that would be circular), and I judged the constant tiny and unlikely to drift.

symbols.name: stripDomainScaffolding
symbols.sig: function stripDomainScaffolding(q: string): string

symbols.name: extractNameFragment
symbols.sig: function extractNameFragment(q: string): string
doc: I isolate the name-shaped remainder of a query for the phonetic fallback (e.g. "when is diwali in 2024" -> "diwali"). It is separate from leftoverAfterStrip in parser.ts, which serves a different purpose (the hijack guard) and must NOT strip question-framing words: there, a bare leftover "when" would correctly still count as "something real is being asked," whereas here it would only get in the way of the name match.

symbols.name: findHolidayNamePhonetic
symbols.sig: export async function findHolidayNamePhonetic( rawQuery: string, year: number | null,): Promise<string | null>
doc: Phonetic name match. I built it as a self-contained fallback using Postgres's stock fuzzystrmatch extension (dmetaphone) -- see phonetic_setup_final.sql for the migration, which was actually installed and tested locally (not just written) before this was wired in: 4 of 5 real corpus spelling variants (Shivratri/Shivaratri, Pongal/Pongol, Mohammad/Mohammed, Bhatridwitiya/Bhatridwitya) match correctly; the one confirmed miss (Janmashtami/Janmasthami -- "sh" and "sth" are genuinely different consonant sounds to an English-oriented algorithm) is covered separately via an explicit alias in that same migration.

It requires holidaymaster.name_phonetic to exist and be populated (see the migration). It is safe to ship before that migration runs: if the column/ function isn't there yet, the query throws, is caught, and this simply returns null, identical to having no phonetic layer at all. The moment the migration is applied, this starts working with no further code changes.
